name: Gyudon (Japanese Beef and Onion Rice Bowls)
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Thinly sliced beef simmered with onions over rice. Cheapest possible Japanese beef dish because the meat is sliced paper-thin, which stretches a small amount a long way, and mirin is a board commodity. Distinct from Japanese Ground Beef Curry and from Loco Moco. Confidence: medium on calories with a soft-egg topper. | HARVEST:
OVERRIDE Rice: '2 servings cooked rice (250 g cooked each)' = 500 g cooked x 0.36 = 180 g dry
intro_html: Gyudon is the Japanese lunch counter bowl: paper-thin beef and onions simmered in a sweet soy broth and spooned over rice. It takes about twenty minutes of actual cooking, which makes it the fastest beef dish in this whole lineup. Slicing the meat thin is the budget trick too, because a little beef spread across a lot of surface area feels like a lot of beef. Each bowl runs {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein for about ${{cost_ps}} a serving (at everyday cost).
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Chicken Broth, 1 carton: ~$1.43. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 2 32oz cartons.
Rice, 7 cups dry: ~$1.56. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 2 2lb bags.
Pantry seasonings (salt, black pepper): ~$0.23. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $39.96 across 14 servings, so roughly $2.85 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $45.42 across 14 servings, roughly $3.24 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $11.01 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $56.43. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a bowl (at everyday cost) for steak and rice, which sounds impossible until you see how thin the beef is sliced. That is the entire idea behind gyudon and it has worked in Japan for a hundred years.
shop_smart: Freeze the steak for about 45 minutes before you slice it. Firm meat cuts thin and clean, and thin slices are what make a small amount of beef stretch across fourteen bowls. This one habit is worth more than any coupon.
Mirin and soy sauce are the whole sauce. Both are one-bottle purchases that last for months of cooking, so the per-bowl cost of the flavor here is close to nothing.
Rice is the cheapest calorie in the store. Buy the big bag, not the box, and the price per serving drops to loose change.
Yellow onions are the other half of the dish, not a garnish. They cook down sweet in the broth and add real volume to the bowl for pennies.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Put the steak in the freezer for 30 to 45 minutes until it is firm but not frozen solid, then slice it against the grain as thin as your knife will allow.
Start the rice so it finishes about when the beef does.
Combine the chicken broth, mirin, soy sauce, and sugar in a wide skillet and bring it to a simmer. Taste it. That broth is what the whole bowl tastes like, so adjust the sugar and soy now.
Add the sliced onions and simmer them for 5 to 7 minutes until they turn soft and translucent.

Lay the beef into the simmering broth in batches, separating the slices as you go, and cook just until the pink disappears. Two minutes is plenty. Overcooked gyudon beef goes tough and stringy, and there is no coming back from it.
Skim any foam off the top, season with a little salt and pepper, and scatter the sliced green onions over the pan.
Let it sit off the heat for five minutes so the beef soaks up the broth before you portion.
portion_html: Weigh the cooked rice into the containers first so every bowl gets the same base, then set the beef pan on the scale, subtract the empty weight you wrote down, and divide by 14. Spoon a little of the broth over each one, since that is where most of the flavor is. Every bowl lands at {{cal}} calories.

steps: Firm the steak in the freezer, then slice it paper thin against the grain.
Simmer chicken broth, mirin, soy sauce, and sugar in a wide skillet.
Add the sliced onions and cook until soft and translucent.
Add the beef in batches and cook just until the pink is gone, then finish with green onions.
Weigh rice and beef into 14 containers with a spoonful of broth each.
